Five additional Lean propositions establish rational floor and half-up rounding prop-

Later observations also require careful dating. A new private fact, an old law newly
added to the collection, and a document published after the method was frozen are
recorded separately.
Declared publication dates do not become externally attested
timestamps. The current frozen method has no future observations, and the prepared
full-document model comparison has no fresh responses under this increment’s offline
execution. Neither missing result is replaced by successful development tests.
2.5 New prospectuses: payment, scope and external
law
A bond can promise repayment at its principal amount while another provision allows
an authority to reduce that claim. Equally, a document can describe a reduction of out-
standing principal because the investor has already received part of the money. These
sentences can look similar to a text classifier, but they describe different changes in the
investor’s rights. The distinction must be settled before the resulting product classifica-
tion is used in a selling decision.
On 4 October 2026, the unchanged prospectus reader was exercised on 24 newly ac-
quired public PDFs. Twenty were issue-specific documents and four were programme
or base prospectuses. They represented 16 issuer families; several documents covered
multiple series, and the Ecuador and Volcan pairs included an initial offering and a later
tap of the same series. The reader abstained on 21 documents and returned three con-
ditional positive readings. An abstention means that its premises remained unresolved,
not that the bond was found to lack a loss mechanism. One positive used demonstrably
incorrect supporting clauses. Appendix B identifies every document, its source date, re-
tained PDF and observed result.
2.5.1 A smaller outstanding balance need not be a loss
Mizuho Markets Cayman’s August 2026 programme provides the clearest error. Its
form of final terms says that amortizing notes are partially redeemed at the specified
Amortization Amount and that their outstanding principal is reduced accordingly. A
neighbouring zero-coupon option likewise reduces outstanding principal upon payment

of the amortization amount. Both passages became principal-write-down witnesses in
the reader’s positive answer.1
The payment relation explains why that inference is wrong. In a simple illustration, an
investor owed 100 receives 20 and retains a claim for 80; the reduction records repay-
ment. If 20 of an unpaid claim is extinguished, the investor instead retains 80 without
having received the missing 20. The programme passage describes the first relation.
Recognising the verb reduced without the payment that causes the reduction loses the
distinction. Moreover, these passages are unselected form options. Correctly interpret-
ing one option would still not establish which terms govern a particular issued bond.
Ethniki’s September 2026 restricted Tier 1 notes supply a contrasting principal-loss
clause. Their Prevailing Principal Amount may be Written Down, and redemption can
occur at that reduced amount without a later entitlement to the difference. The reader
found this mechanism but left 57 candidate records unresolved. MUFG’s August 2026
base prospectus similarly states that the principal of Subordinated Notes is written down
to zero following a Non-Viability Event. That clause supports a reading of the subordi-
nated option; it does not classify every note issued under the programme. 2
2.5.2 The principal must belong to the right instrument
A provision’s subject matters as much as its action. All three unresolved records in
EDF’s 2023 perpetual-note document discussed separate OCEANE convertible bonds
due in 2024. An apparent exclusion of principal write-down elsewhere in the same
document applied to Exchanged Notes or Varied Notes. It was therefore unsuitable as an
exhaustive negative statement about the original notes. Volcan’s 2025 memorandum
supplied an even sharper contrast: several candidate forfeiture clauses concerned min-
ing concessions or water licences. Those assets can affect the issuer’s financial position,
but forfeiture of a mining concession is not itself cancellation of the principal of its
Notes.3
Missing context can also produce a misleading impression of completeness. Zurich Fi-
nance Ireland’s eight-page July 2026 pricing supplement identifies senior notes and a
redemption amount, but expressly incorporates the 19 May 2026 base prospectus. The
isolated-document reader left debt status unknown while marking its local clause cov-
erage complete. Both PDFs had been downloaded, but the diagnostic input had not
declared their dependency. The useful repair is to connect the correct issue documents
and interpret their labelled fields. The absence of a clause from a short supplement
cannot establish that the complete terms contain no such clause. 4

2.5.3 The applicable legal power needs a date and a subject
HPB’s July 2026 senior preferred notes illustrate the next step beyond a repayment
promise. The disclosure says that an authority may order a write-down of the Notes or
convert them into CET1 instruments, and describes cancellation of liabilities including
the Notes. The reader left these clauses unresolved. The source supports investigation
of a principal-loss power; the phrase CET1 instruments still needs interpretation before it
can establish the narrower common-share conversion feature. An exclusion of contrac-
tual loss terms in the definition of replacement Qualifying Securities does not negate
statutory powers over the original Notes.5
Insurance-resolution language shows why the date cannot be inferred from the pres-
ence of a legal reference. AXA’s June 2024 prospectus calls the Insurance Recovery and
Resolution Directive proposal a proposed measure and says If adopted. SCOR’s June
2026 prospectus describes national implementation and application in January 2027
and states that French implementation was pending. These passages disclose a possi-
ble future change. They do not, by themselves, establish an already applicable power at
the relevant assessment date. Existing contractual provisions and other national pow-
ers must be examined separately.6
Nor is the question confined to regulatory capital. Prudentia’s AirBlu compartment
terms extinguish the right to further amounts after the compartment assets have been
realised and distributed. Orange describes court restructuring capable of binding dis-
senting creditor classes. Whether these mechanisms satisfy the declared principal-loss
predicate requires analysis of the unpaid claim and the authority for the change. Nei-
ther can be excluded merely by calling it ordinary credit risk or observing that the se-
curity is not bank capital.7
The 24-document exercise therefore identifies several different engineering tasks: inter-
pret payment and extinguishment correctly; bind a clause to its instrument; assemble
the issue documents; and establish which law applies when. The sources and results
remain preserved with the original reader unchanged. The findings are based on in-
spected extracted text and are provisional pending rendered-source and independent
legal review. Passing software tests cannot supply those missing interpretations.
2.5.4 Three further historical documents
A further search retained three historical documents for testing the boundary between
contractual promises and local-law investigation. Banco Espírito Santo’s final terms
dated 6 May 2014 identify EUR 750 million of 2.625 percent senior notes due 8 May 2017,
Series 36, tranche 1. Page 2 promises redemption at 100 percent of nominal amount,

subject to the stated prior-redemption and cancellation qualifications. Page 1 incorpo-
rates the July 2013 prospectus and four dated supplements. Thus the visible senior-
status and repayment fields are precise contractual evidence, but the five-page final
terms alone cannot answer a question about later Portuguese resolution measures or
their recognition abroad.8 The proposed follow-up is to match the exact security to the
relevant Portuguese measures and judicial decisions. That matching has not yet been
established by the retained external-law sources.
The Greek document gives a directly visible example of a broad promise qualified by
another jurisdiction’s law. Its March 2008 offering circular covers a EUR 600 million
tap of inflation-linked notes due in 2057. Condition 4 floors the contractual redemp-
tion amount at principal. Condition 14 selects English law and contains a broad waiver
of immunity, but then expressly subjects execution and attachment of the Republic’s
property to international conventions and Greek law. A repayment entitlement, juris-
diction over a lawsuit and access to assets for enforcement are therefore three different
propositions. The country name also cannot justify attaching a Greek-law restructuring
rule to these English-law notes without checking that rule’s scope and the actual series
history.9 No specific seizure, restructuring outcome or recovery amount is established
by that qualification alone.
The Slovenian search produced SID Bank’s March 2011 memorandum, rather than an
NLB subordinated issue. It describes a EUR 350 million tap of 3 percent notes due in
2015 and an unconditional, irrevocable state guarantee. Its description of the guarantee
refers to article 13 of the Slovenian Export and Development Bank Act, transactions
under articles 11–12 and a creditor’s written request. The Notes themselves use English
law. The correct investigation must therefore establish the statutory guarantee’s scope
and conditions, while keeping SID Bank distinct from another Slovenian bank with
different instruments or intervention history.10 This document is retained as an issuer-
and-guarantee control. It does not demonstrate that the guarantee was overridden or
that these notes suffered a principal write-down.
These new documents extend the tests in two directions. The BES terms provide a con-
crete repayment promise requiring a later-event investigation. The Greek and SID doc-
uments prevent that investigation from becoming a country-wide presumption: gov-
erning law, enforcement limits, issuer identity and the statutory guarantee each have
to be bound to the particular claim. The first retrieval round did not yield readable
judgments. The extended search has now retained the relevant European judgments
and the BES base prospectuses and named supplements. These sources make the legal
questions more precise, while leaving the exact identifier-to-measure link open for the
May 2014 issue.

2.5.5 A repayment promise after a liability moves
The clearest new comparison begins with another BES issue. Final terms dated 14 July
2011 promise redemption at par of EUR 81.4 million of senior notes, paying 6.875 per-
cent and maturing on 15 July 2016. The scanned pages identify Series 23, Portuguese
law and ISIN PTBEQBOM0010. They incorporate the 3 November 2010 base prospectus
and six supplements, all now retained. The 2013 base used by the two later BES issues
is a different edition; its cover cannot silently replace the earlier terms.11
The Court of Justice’s 2024 Novo Banco judgment describes a senior bond with that
coupon and maturity. Its purchaser acquired the bond in November 2014, after the
original transfer of liabilities to Novo Banco, and received the following year’s coupon.
At maturity, Novo Banco paid neither the next coupon nor principal. It relied on the
Bank of Portugal’s 29 December 2015 decisions transferring the liability back to BES.
Thus a historical coupon payment cannot establish who remains liable at a later date.
The court describes the bond by name, coupon and maturity but does not print its ISIN.
The retained final terms are consequently a strong candidate match; the missing Por-
tuguese Annex 2B still prevents an exact identifier-level conclusion.12
Timing changes the recognition question. In the 2024 case the measures preceded the
Spanish proceedings. The Court held that the omitted publication required by arti-
cle 6 of Directive 2001/24 did not itself prevent recognition, while preserving effective
access to an appeal in the home state. In C-504/19, by contrast, the later retransfer
sought to change liability during proceedings in which the claimant had already ob-
tained a favourable decision. The Court rejected unconditional recognition that would
retroactively remove the defendant and call those decisions into question. That dispute
concerned a share-sale agreement, not the senior bond. A useful engine must retain
both the procedural dates and the type of claim; a single rule saying that all retransfers
succeed or all fail would misread these decisions.13
2.5.6 Payment can be delayed, reduced or enforced elsewhere
HETA’s notices separate changes that a loss classifier could easily collapse. The March
2015 notice describes amended maturities: the affected amounts would not yet become
due and payable. The April 2016 notice reports a later decree reducing eligible nonsub-
ordinated liabilities, including interest due through 28 February 2015, to 46.02 percent
of par. Interest falling due after that date was reduced to zero, and the latest maturity
was set at 31 December 2023. A remaining amount of 46.02 percent corresponds to a
53.98 percent reduction in that stated bucket. The notice adds that the legal relation-

ship and trading could continue. Continuing existence and tradability therefore do not
establish unchanged payment rights.14
Adriatica Finance offers a different kind of local-law problem. Its 2007 securitisation
finances claims arising from the Abruzzo region’s payment undertakings for health-
care liabilities. The prospectus describes those undertakings as irrevocable and un-
conditional, but also explains why obtaining payment can be harder than reading that
promise suggests. Certain public funds cannot be attached if the stated statutory con-
ditions are met. Execution against the region is subject to a 120-day period after no-
tification of the enforceable instrument and payment request. Accelerating the Notes
does not accelerate the region’s remaining scheduled payments. These qualifications
concern available assets and timing; they must not be recast as immediate principal
cancellation.15
The same prospectus distinguishes maturity from extinguishment. If funds are insuf-
ficient at December 2021 maturity, unpaid amounts remain outstanding until the last
business day of December 2026. Condition 7(b) then cancels outstanding amounts in
the absence of the issuer’s gross negligence or wilful misconduct. Neither the earlier
maturity nor the later cancellation can be interpreted without its condition. The seller’s
letter of undertaking also expressly disclaims being a guarantee; public receivables and
transaction support are not interchangeable with a guarantee of the Notes.16
2.5.7 A foreign-law objection can fail
Dana Gas supplies a useful control against assuming that local law always defeats a
payment promise. The 2017 English judgment addressed a transaction with UAE-law
and English-law documents. For a preliminary issue, the court assumed without decid-
ing the alleged invalidity under UAE law. It nevertheless held the English-law purchase
undertaking valid and enforceable, having examined its construction, allocation of risk,
mistake and public policy. An engine must identify which obligation a particular law
governs and whether the court adopted a proposition as a finding or only as an assump-
tion for argument.17
Lloyds’ enhanced capital notes expose another distinction. Changes to regulatory cap-
ital requirements were held by the majority to satisfy a Capital Disqualification Event,
enabling optional early redemption. The conversion trigger was a separate provision.

of an unidentified HETA security.

The judgment does not establish that the notes were converted or their principal writ-
ten down. The dissent disagreed about redeemability, so extracting an isolated judicial
sentence without its author and disposition could reverse the result.18
The Ukrainian sovereign-note decision illustrates a procedural limit.
The Supreme
Court refused summary judgment and allowed the specified alleged force-based duress
defence to proceed to trial. That is neither a finding that duress occurred nor a final can-
cellation of the debt. The majority rejected the capacity, authority and countermeasure
defences. Those different dispositions belong in the answer together.19
2.5.8 What the additional tests actually found
The extension records 30 distinct questions, supported by 51 checked passages, across
offering documents, judgments and issuer notices. They include the differences be-
tween a state-aid communication and a national power, shares and bonds in prospec-
tus litigation, and deposit guarantees and investor compensation. The companion gives
each question an identifier, its source and the inference it must prevent.
Seven new offering PDFs were submitted to the unchanged reader. All seven produced
abstentions, with 29 unresolved clause records and no runtime errors. Three additional
page-limited probes reproduced a more specific error: clauses extinguishing unpaid
principal were classified as ordinary cancellation following redemption or repurchase.
Two occur in Adriano Lease Sec.’s conditions, including cancellation after a servicer cer-
tificate and representative notice; the third is Adriatica’s later Cancellation Date. The
original conditions preserve exceptions that a repaired interpretation must carry for-
ward.20
This is a wrong clause classification relative to the described unpaid extinguishment.
It did not produce a complete negative issue answer in these runs: the reader still ab-
stained. The result therefore identifies a concrete repair target without measuring pop-
ulation accuracy. The remaining legal questions are source-supported specifications for
an integrated evaluator and independent adjudication; they are not 30 reported engine
successes or 30 proven instances of investor loss.
2.6 Marketing rules require exceptions and judgment
The October 2023 distributor circular examines additional returns and incentives,
redemption restrictions and marketing of fund-related services.

Appendix B
B.3 How to reproduce and interpret this record
The protected run used commit 2d6b737b plus 293 archived source files, including then-
uncommitted repairs. It completed in 16.063 seconds on the existing CPU environment,
with a 60-second guard per document and no classifier tuning after selection. Across
all 24 documents there were 21 abstentions, three conditional positives and no runtime
errors. The three focused harness checks and 909 prospectus regression tests passed;
those checks establish software and preservation properties, not independent legal cor-
rectness.
The source set has 24 distinct hashes and 16 issuer families, below the original prefer-
ence of at least 20 families. Orange had previous catalogue discovery exposure. The
engine received whole-document diagnostic selections; that choice deliberately tests
irrelevant text and unselected options, but does not establish their legal applicability.
These distinctions prevent an abstention count from being presented as an error rate.

B.5.2 Judgments, notices and the limits of their holdings
The oﬀicial 2024 Novo Banco judgment, C-498/22 to C-500/22 records a bond retransfer
and nonpayment (paras. 58–63), and addresses recognition of measures adopted be-
fore proceedings (paras. 89–97). The 2021 judgment, C-504/19 concerns a share-sale
liability changed during pending proceedings (paras. 49, 59–66). Goldman Sachs v Novo
Banco, [2018] UKSC 34 concerns the Oak loan and recognition of a determination that
its liability had never transferred (paras. 21–34, PDF pp. 9–12). These are three distinct
disputes.
In Kotnik, C-526/14, ECLI:EU:C:2016:570, the Banking Communication cannot impose
independent obligations on Member States (para. 44). The burden-sharing discussion
preserves qualifications, including the no-creditor-worse-off principle (para. 77), and
distinguishes authority-adopted measures from private arrangements for the Direc-
tive 2001/24 classification (para. 110). Kuhn, C-308/17, ECLI:EU:C:2018:911, addresses
the civil-and-commercial-matters jurisdiction boundary, not the merits of a particular
English-law bond’s haircut (para. 44).
Banco Santander, C-410/20, ECLI:EU:C:2022:351, addresses specified prospectus dam-
ages and nullity claims after a total share write-down (para. 51).
Its discussion of
compensation compares resolution with normal insolvency; it does not guarantee the
original investment’s value (paras. 48–50). Indėlių ir investicijų draudimas, C-671/13,
ECLI:EU:C:2015:418, makes negotiability material to deposit-certificate exclusion
(paras. 38–40).
Exclusion from deposit protection does not automatically exclude
investor protection, whose own conditions still apply (paras. 47–52). In particular,
article 2(2) of Directive 97/9 concerns the inability to return money or instruments
held in connection with investment business. The judgment is not a general guarantee
against an issuer’s credit default.
